column2: A drawing specifies 0.80-inch pitch for six rivets in one row. How far apart are the end centers?
column3: 4.00 inches
column4: 4.80 inches
column5: 5.60 inches
column6: 3.20 inches
column7: Pitch is the center-to-center spacing within a row. Six centers create five intervals, so the end centers are 5 times 0.80 inch apart.

column2: What dimension on a riveted patch is measured perpendicular to two adjacent rows?
column3: Transverse pitch
column4: Longitudinal pitch
column5: Edge distance
column6: Rivet grip
column7: Transverse pitch measures the spacing between rows. Pitch along a row measures the distance between successive rivet centers.

column2: A drawing gives edge distance for a skin repair. From which points is it measured?
column3: Nearest hole center to sheet edge
column4: Nearest hole rim to sheet edge
column5: Rivet head edge to sheet edge
column6: Adjacent hole centers along the edge
column7: Edge distance uses the center of the nearest rivet hole as its datum. The rim or head gives a different dimension.

column2: Two sheets measuring 0.040 and 0.063 inch are clamped together. What is the solid rivet grip length?
column3: 0.103 inch
column4: 0.023 inch
column5: 0.080 inch
column6: 0.126 inch
column7: Grip is the combined thickness of the joined material. The extra shank needed to form the shop head is added separately.

column2: Which change to a flush rivet hole is made by dimpling the sheet?
column3: Forming a recess with matched dies
column4: Cutting a recess with a tapered cutter
column5: Sizing the bore with a fluted reamer
column6: Compressing the rivet tail with a squeezer
column7: Dimpling displaces the sheet between matched male and female dies. Machine countersinking cuts the recess.

column2: Which feature of a microstop countersink produces consistent recesses across a row of holes?
column3: Adjustable depth stop
column4: Interchangeable pilot diameter
column5: Cutter's included angle
column6: Cutting flute clearance
column7: The stop limits penetration to the selected depth. The cutter angle sets the shape of the seat.

column2: A drilled fastener hole needs a finer finish at its final diameter. Which tool fits that operation?
column3: A correctly sized reamer
column4: A piloted countersink
column5: An offset rivet set
column6: A center punch
column7: A reamer finishes an existing hole to size. A countersink works the seating surface around its opening.

column2: Which tool reacts against the tail of a solid rivet while a gun strikes the manufactured head?
column3: Bucking bar
column4: Rivet set
column5: Draw punch
column6: Rivet cutter
column7: The bucking bar's mass opposes the blows and helps upset the tail into the shop head. The rivet set contacts the manufactured head.

column2: A released flange opens slightly after bending in a brake. What material behavior explains the change?
column3: Elastic recovery after forming
column4: Plastic flow while clamped
column5: Thermal expansion during service
column6: Workpiece slip before clamping
column7: Spring-back is the recovery of some of the imposed bend once the forming load is removed.

column2: Which brake feature makes it possible to form the remaining side of a partly finished box?
column3: Removable fingers on the upper jaw
column4: An adjustable stop on the bending leaf
column5: A longer handle on the clamping lever
column6: A radius shim along the bending edge
column7: Removing interfering fingers gives the previously formed sides clearance. A continuous clamping jaw can obstruct the final bend.

column2: Where does a mechanic align the marked sight line for an ordinary bend on a cornice brake?
column3: Directly beneath the clamping bar edge
column4: At the center of the bend allowance
column5: Along the back edge of the brake bed
column6: At the outer edge of the bending leaf
column7: The sight line locates the sheet against the edge of the clamping bar before the leaf forms the bend.

column2: Which material characteristic is necessary for inspecting a fitting by magnetic particle testing?
column3: It is ferromagnetic
column4: Its surface readily absorbs penetrant
column5: It transmits high-frequency sound
column6: Its density strongly attenuates X-rays
column7: Magnetic particle testing needs ferromagnetic material. A discontinuity disturbs the applied field and can produce a visible particle pattern.

column2: Why can an eddy current inspection work on an aluminum skin without magnetizing it?
column3: The metal conducts induced electrical currents
column4: The alloy retains a residual magnetic field
column5: Its grain refracts sound at the crack face
column6: Its surface draws liquid into narrow openings
column7: The probe induces currents in electrically conductive material. Changes in those currents can indicate a discontinuity.

column2: An authorized repair calls for GTAW with filler. How is the filler supplied?
column3: Separately from the nonconsumable electrode
column4: From the flux coating on a steel electrode
column5: By melting the tip of the tungsten electrode
column6: Through a continuously fed electrode wire
column7: In gas tungsten arc welding the tungsten sustains the arc. Filler, when required, is supplied separately.

column2: What provides filler metal in a typical gas metal arc weld?
column3: Wire electrode fed through the torch
column4: A nonconsumable tungsten rod
column5: Flux released from the gas nozzle
column6: Copper tips clamped against the sheet
column7: The GMAW arc melts the wire electrode as well as the work. The continuously fed wire contributes metal to the weld.

column2: Why does a GTAW torch supply argon around the molten pool?
column3: To protect the molten metal against oxidation
column4: To carry filler from the rod into the joint
column5: To conduct current back to the power supply
column6: To set the final hardness of the parent alloy
column7: Argon shields the molten metal from air and helps prevent oxide formation. The electrode and work form the electrical circuit.

column2: Which process joins overlapping sheets by passing current through material held between two clamped copper electrodes?
column3: Resistance spot welding
column4: Gas tungsten arc welding
column5: Shielded metal arc welding
column6: Oxyacetylene welding
column7: The sheets heat because they resist the current flowing between the electrodes. Pressure holds the parts in contact as the spot forms.

column2: What is a rosette weld intended to connect in a tubular airframe repair?
column3: An internal reinforcing liner to the outside tube
column4: Two tube ends meeting at a butt joint
column5: Adjacent flanges of a sheet metal channel
column6: Two parallel tubes along their contact line
column7: A rosette weld fuses an inner reinforcing tube to the outer member through an opening in the outer wall.

column2: Which measurement can be verified on a marked sheet before any fasteners are installed?
column3: Hole locations relative to the edges of the patch
column4: Final shop head diameter on each driven rivet
column5: Actual flushness of the completed fasteners
column6: Measured distortion after the last rivet is driven
column7: Layout establishes the pattern, size, spacing, and edge distance before the holes are drilled. The remaining measurements evaluate the installed repair.

column2: Why check minimum spacing and edge distance again when a repair calls for a larger replacement rivet?
column3: Required clearances may depend on shank diameter
column4: A larger shop head decreases the measured sheet thickness
column5: The larger shank moves the existing hole center
column6: A larger rivet changes the alloy temper of the patch
column7: Repair spacing and edge-distance limits often use multiples of diameter. Enlarging a hole keeps its center but can leave insufficient distance under the applicable criteria.

column2: Inspection finds short buckled lines across the grain of a wooden spar after overload. Which defect fits?
column3: Compression failure
column4: Longitudinal shake
column5: Pitch pocket
column6: Mineral streak
column7: Overstressed wood fibers can buckle on a plane across their length. Fine compression failures can appear as hairline streaks across the grain.

column2: A longitudinal crack in aircraft wood follows the boundary between annual rings. What is it called?
column3: Shake
column4: Check
column5: Spike knot
column6: Cross grain
column7: A shake normally separates adjacent growth rings. A check generally crosses them.

column2: A wooden panel bulges around a break in its varnish. Which underlying condition is most likely?
column3: Moisture damage beneath the coating
column4: Normal variation in annual ring width
column5: Compression failure during tree felling
column6: Excessive grain slope at a scarf joint
column7: A break in the protective coating can admit water. Swelling or warping is a reason to investigate the structure for damage or decay.

column2: Which property makes a continuous gusset useful on a wooden truss rib?
column3: It stiffens the cap strip against buckling
column4: It transfers engine torque into the spar
column5: It fixes the spacing between the wing spars
column6: It sets the wing's angle of incidence
column7: The continuous gusset supports the truss and cap strip in the plane of the rib with little added weight.

column2: Which direction is the bias when cutting a patch from woven aircraft covering fabric?
column3: Diagonally across warp and fill
column4: Parallel to the mill-finished edge
column5: Across the width along a fill thread
column6: Lengthwise along the warp threads
column7: Warp runs lengthwise and fill across the width. A bias cut crosses those directions diagonally.

column2: Why is an inspection ring bonded to a fabric covering over a designated access location?
column3: To support the edge of a future access opening
column4: To distribute rib lacing loads into the covering
column5: To maintain fabric tension across a glued seam
column6: To vent water collected in the bottom of a bay
column7: The ring provides a stable rim when the inside fabric is cut for inspection. A cover closes the opening afterward.

column2: A fabric-covered wing retains water after rain. Which installation detail is most directly relevant?
column3: Drain openings at the specified low points
column4: Finishing tape width over the rib lacing
column5: Position of the upper inspection covers
column6: Warp alignment at the leading edge
column7: Drain grommets or approved reinforced openings allow rain or condensation to escape. Their locations come from the applicable covering instructions.

column2: What determines whether clips may replace the original lacing used to attach a wing covering?
column3: Approval for that change in attachment method
column4: Matching tensile ratings on the cord and clips
column5: Equal spacing between existing attachment points
column6: Use of clips on another model with similar ribs
column7: The FAA handbook calls for the original attachment method or approval for a change. Similar dimensions or use on another model do not establish approval.

column2: What does a dull response during a tap survey of thin honeycomb face sheets warrant investigating?
column3: A local void or delamination
column4: A fully bonded area matching sound structure
column5: Uneven pigment in an intact topcoat
column6: A small change in surface gloss
column7: A sound area usually rings more clearly under comparable conditions. A dull response is an indication requiring evaluation under the repair data.

column2: A thick composite laminate looks intact after impact. Why can additional approved nondestructive inspection be needed?
column3: Surface rebound can conceal damage inside the laminate
column4: Visual inspection measures damage depth but misses its width
column5: Thickness prevents stress spreading between adjacent plies
column6: Impact always leaves matching marks on the opposite surface
column7: Composite surfaces can rebound after an impact and conceal damage beyond the visible mark. The structural repair manual guides the choice of inspection method.

column2: A prepreg roll is out of frozen storage twice, for 50 and 80 minutes. What out time is recorded?
column3: 130 minutes
column4: 80 minutes
column5: 65 minutes
column6: 30 minutes
column7: Out time accumulates across exposures. Returning material to the freezer between uses does not erase the earlier interval.

column2: Why should frozen prepreg thaw in its sealed bag before it is opened?
column3: To keep moisture from condensing on the material
column4: To prevent resin flowing into the breather cloth
column5: To complete the first stage of the cure cycle
column6: To allow the remaining out time to reset
column7: A cold roll exposed to humid air can collect moisture. The closed bag isolates the material while it warms.

column2: What does checking a vacuum bag for leaks establish before curing a bonded repair?
column3: The bag can maintain the required pressure difference
column4: The resin has reached its allowed service temperature
column5: The reinforcement has the specified fiber orientation
column6: The adhesive has achieved its final cured strength
column7: Air leaks can disrupt consolidation and introduce air during cure. A leak check assesses the bag's integrity before the cure cycle.

column2: Why monitor the coolest thermocouple as well as the hottest during a bonded repair cure?
column3: One region may remain undercured while another overheats
column4: The resin's batch identity changes with the temperature range
column5: The average reading reveals the repair's final bond strength
column6: The hottest reading alone measures vacuum under the bag
column7: The approved cure specification governs exposure across the repair. Tracking both extremes helps identify insufficient heat and excessive temperature.

column2: An acrylic window develops a network of fine surface fissures. Which defect describes this appearance?
column3: Crazing
column4: Delamination
column5: Chafing
column6: Indentation
column7: Crazing consists of tiny cracks or fissures in the plastic surface. Stress and incompatible chemicals can cause it.

column2: Why are transparent thermoplastic sheets kept away from heaters while awaiting installation?
column3: Elevated temperatures can distort their shape
column4: Condensation can soften the plastic above its forming range
column5: Thermal cycling changes the sheet's original grain direction
column6: Radiant heat hardens the surface before installation
column7: Thermoplastics soften when heated. The FAA advises cool, dry storage away from heat sources and paint fumes.

column2: Which device guides an almost straight control cable through a bulkhead opening without chafing the cable?
column3: Fairlead
column4: Turnbuckle
column5: Cable quadrant
column6: Bellcrank
column7: A fairlead surrounds the cable where it passes a structure. A pulley handles a significant change of direction.

column2: What function does a guard serve where a flight control cable passes around a pulley?
column3: Retaining the slack line in its groove
column4: Setting the cable's initial rigging tension
column5: Adjusting the angular travel of the pulley
column6: Holding the control surface at neutral
column7: A cable can slacken as conditions change. The guard keeps it from jumping the groove.

column2: How does a cable tensiometer obtain its reading on an installed control cable?
column3: By measuring the force to deflect a supported span
column4: By measuring cable stretch over its entire run
column5: By measuring the torque at the nearest turnbuckle
column6: By measuring the load at the control stop
column7: The instrument presses a riser against cable supported by anvils. The force required for that offset corresponds to tension using the appropriate calibration.

column2: Which environmental reading determines the target value on a cable rigging chart?
column3: Ambient temperature near the cable run
column4: Local barometric pressure at cable height
column5: Relative humidity in the hangar
column6: Wind speed at the wingtip
column7: Cable and airframe materials expand differently. The rigging chart relates the specified tension to temperature.

column2: Why does a control cable turnbuckle use opposite thread directions at its two ends?
column3: Barrel rotation adjusts length with both ends attached
column4: Cable tension is carried by a single terminal
column5: Both terminals back out whenever the control moves
column6: The barrel acts as a stop at maximum control travel
column7: One end has right-hand threads and the other has left-hand threads. Turning the barrel moves both terminals inward or outward.

column2: Which component transmits a twisting input along its length in a mechanical control system?
column3: Torque tube
column4: Push-pull rod
column5: Tension cable
column6: Pulley guard
column7: A torque tube carries rotary motion between linkages. A push-pull rod carries movement along its axis.

column2: Which part of an adjustable push rod sets the distance between its attachment centers?
column3: Threaded rod end
column4: Pulley bearing
column5: Control stop
column6: Cable shackle
column7: The rod-end fitting threads into the tube assembly, allowing adjustment of its effective length. The locknut secures the setting.

column2: During rigging, why are controls and bellcranks held at their specified neutral positions?
column3: To preserve the reference while cable tension is set
column4: To establish maximum travel from stop contact
column5: To unload the control surface for static balancing
column6: To measure the full stroke of a trim actuator
column7: Rigging pins or blocks establish the neutral reference. The tension is then adjusted without shifting the controls from that reference.

column2: Which measurement establishes whether the stops on a rigged elevator give the specified movement?
column3: Angular travel each way from neutral
column4: Cable tension with the elevator centered
column5: Hinge moment with the trim tab faired
column6: Longitudinal alignment of the stabilizer
column7: Control stops limit travel. Compare each direction from neutral with the manufacturer's specified range using the prescribed measuring equipment.

column2: A repainted aileron moves freely. Which separate check addresses its susceptibility to flutter?
column3: Mass balance about the hinge axis
column4: Hinge line alignment with the wing spar
column5: Cable tension at full travel
column6: Trim tab angle at neutral
column7: Even when movement is free, the mass distribution relative to the hinge can be outside limits. The manufacturer's balance specification addresses this source of flutter.

column2: Which tab uses aerodynamic force to move the primary surface in response to pilot input?
column3: Servo tab
column4: Adjustable trim tab
column5: Antiservo tab
column6: Balance tab
column7: A servo tab commands movement of the main surface through aerodynamic force on the tab. A balance tab primarily reduces the effort required to move the main surface.

column2: A stabilator's trailing-edge tab increases pilot effort as deflection grows. Which behavior identifies an antiservo tab?
column3: It deflects in the same direction as the stabilator
column4: It moves opposite to the stabilator's displacement
column5: It remains fixed relative to the fuselage centerline
column6: It locks flush when the stabilator leaves neutral
column7: An antiservo tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator and increases control feel. This helps limit excessive pitch sensitivity.

column2: Who has primary responsibility for keeping a US civil aircraft airworthy under 14 CFR 91.403?
column3: Registered owner or operator
column4: Mechanic who signed the last annual
column5: Inspector who issued the original certificate
column6: Manufacturer holding the type certificate
column7: Section 91.403 assigns primary responsibility to the owner or operator, including compliance with applicable airworthiness directives.

column2: A standard-category private airplane had its annual on May 8. Through when is that annual normally current the next year?
column3: May 31
column4: May 7
column5: April 30
column6: June 8
column7: For an aircraft under the ordinary annual requirement, the interval is 12 calendar months. The inspection remains current through the last day of the corresponding month.

column2: Which flight instruction arrangement triggers the ordinary Part 91 100-hour inspection requirement?
column3: Paid instruction in an airplane supplied by the instructor
column4: Paid instruction in an airplane supplied by the student
column5: Unpaid instruction in the student's private airplane
column6: Unpaid instruction in an airplane supplied by the instructor
column7: The rule covers flight instruction for hire in an aircraft provided by the person giving instruction. It also covers carrying persons other than crewmembers for hire.

column2: An airplane used 6 extra hours en route to its 100-hour inspection. How many hours remain until the next one?
column3: 94 hours
column4: 100 hours
column5: 106 hours
column6: 90 hours
column7: The permitted en route excess counts toward the next interval. Six excess hours leave 94 after the inspection.

column2: Who receives an aircraft owner's written request to use a Part 91 progressive inspection program?
column3: Responsible FAA Flight Standards office
column4: Manufacturer's technical publications department
column5: Repair station maintaining the aircraft records
column6: FAA Aircraft Registration Branch
column7: Section 91.409(d) directs the owner or operator to submit the written request to the responsible Flight Standards office.

column2: In a progressive inspection, what separates a detailed examination from a routine one?
column3: Disassembly as needed for a thorough examination
column4: Recording the total aircraft time after the work
column5: Use of a signed checklist for each inspection
column6: Scheduling the examination by hours in service
column7: Routine checks are visual insofar as practicable without disassembly. A detailed examination includes the disassembly necessary to examine the item thoroughly.

column2: An owner ends phased inspections under section 91.409(d). What establishes the next annual's due date?
column3: Date all components last received a complete inspection
column4: Date the last routine phase inspection was performed
column5: Date of written notice to the FAA
column6: Date the owner selected a new mechanic
column7: Section 91.409(d) measures the annual interval from the last complete progressive inspection. A routine phase plus a detailed inspection of a few components is insufficient.

column2: A mechanic designs a checklist for an annual inspection on a fixed-wing airplane. What governs minimum coverage?
column3: Part 43 Appendix D scope and detail
column4: Tasks listed on the last discrepancy sheet
column5: Inspection tasks completed by the current owner
column6: Items requiring lubrication in the maintenance manual
column7: Section 43.15(c) allows a mechanic's own checklist but prescribes its content. Appendix D sets the scope and detail for the aircraft, with additional provisions for rotorcraft where applicable.

column2: What aircraft time belongs in the record entry for a completed annual inspection?
column3: Total aircraft time in service
column4: Time flown since the previous annual
column5: Time since engine overhaul
column6: Hours still available on the next 100-hour interval
column7: Section 43.11 requires the inspection date and aircraft total time in service, alongside the type of inspection and the other required entries.

column2: An annual inspection ends with an unairworthy finding. What must the inspector provide the owner or lessee?
column3: A signed, dated list of discrepancies
column4: A replacement standard airworthiness certificate
column5: An amended type certificate data sheet
column6: An application for inspection authorization
column7: Section 43.11 requires a signed and dated discrepancy list. The inspection entry records that the aircraft was inspected and that the list was provided.

column2: How long must the owner keep a discrepancy list furnished under 14 CFR 43.11?
column3: Until repair of the defects and approval for return to service
column4: Until the next scheduled annual inspection begins
column5: For 12 calendar months after receiving the list
column6: Until the owner engages someone to perform the repairs
column7: Under section 91.417(b)(3), retention continues until the defects have been repaired and the aircraft has been approved for return to service.

column2: Which item does section 91.417(a)(2) require an owner to retain and pass to a buyer?
column3: Current status of installed life-limited parts
column4: Latest estimate for routine preventive work
column5: Shop work order for a routine oil change
column6: Completed task card for the last tire change
column7: Life-limited part status is one of the records listed in section 91.417(a)(2). The owner retains that group of records and transfers it with the aircraft on sale.

column2: What additional entry is needed in the compliance record for a repetitive airworthiness directive?
column3: Time and date when the next action is required
column4: Labor hours logged during the previous inspection
column5: Time between publication and first compliance
column6: Date the operator first acquired the product
column7: Section 91.417(a)(2)(v) requires this scheduling information in addition to the method of compliance, directive number, and revision date.

column2: A design change prevents accomplishing an applicable AD as written. What permits a different compliance procedure?
column3: FAA approval of a proposed alternative
column4: A revised log entry signed by the aircraft owner
column5: Authorization from the operator's maintenance planner
column6: Acceptance by the shop performing the alteration
column7: A changed product can still fall within an AD. Section 39.17 requires a request for FAA approval when the change affects accomplishment of the required action.

column2: What makes an aircraft fitting a life-limited part under 14 CFR 43.10?
column3: A mandatory replacement limit in the applicable design or maintenance data
column4: A supplier's recommendation for an economic replacement interval
column5: A repair station's normal time between component inspections
column6: A manufacturer's general schedule for cleaning and lubrication
column7: A mandatory replacement limit in the type design, instructions for continued airworthiness, or maintenance manual establishes life-limited status.

column2: A serialized part retires at 12,000 cycles and has accumulated 9,350. How much cycle life remains?
column3: 2,650 cycles
column4: 3,650 cycles
column5: 2,350 cycles
column6: 9,350 cycles
column7: Track life in the unit specified by the applicable limit. Subtracting the accumulated 9,350 cycles from 12,000 leaves 2,650.

column2: A shop tags a removed component under section 43.10(c). Which data identify it and its remaining eligibility?
column3: Part number, serial number, and current life status
column4: Aircraft registration, component model, and time since overhaul
column5: Part number, aircraft serial number, and removal date
column6: Serial number, inspection date, and replacement cost
column7: The tag must identify the particular part and its accumulated life status. An existing tag must be updated, or a new one created, each time the part is removed.

column2: An airplane matches its approved design but has corrosion beyond service limits. Which requirement does it fail?
column3: Condition for safe operation
column4: Conformity to the approved design
column5: Conformity to the registration markings
column6: Eligibility of its type certificate holder
column7: Airworthiness requires conformity to the type design or properly altered condition and condition for safe operation. Current paperwork cannot establish acceptable physical condition.

column2: A pilot reports a hard touchdown. What inspection scope does the FAA identify for this event?
column3: Airframe structure including gear attachments
column4: Tires, wheels, and brakes at the affected gear
column5: Strut extension and tire pressure on all gear
column6: Wheel alignment and local brake line condition
column7: A hard landing can load the airframe as well as the gear. The applicable special inspection evaluates the affected structure under the aircraft's maintenance data.

column2: A baseline airframe configuration is needed for a conformity inspection. Which FAA document is the starting reference?
column3: Type Certificate Data Sheet
column4: Airworthiness Directives Biweekly Report
column5: Mechanic Airman Certification Standards
column6: Aircraft Registration Application
column7: The type certificate data sheet identifies the certificated product and its approved characteristics. Applicable alterations also need to be accounted for when evaluating the aircraft's actual configuration.
